title: The Candy Rocket
summary: Three friends blast off in a rocket made of biscuits and sweets, and up in the sky they meet a little star who needs their help.

scenes.text:
Noa, Tomi and Sami spent a whole Sunday building a spaceship in the back garden.

It wasn't any old spaceship. It was a spaceship made of sweets.

The walls were candy canes, striped red and white. The buttons were lollipops. The door was an enormous biscuit. And in the round window at the top, to be the passengers, they put a row of gummy bears.

"Rule number one," said Noa, very seriously. "No eating the spaceship."

"No eating it," said Sami.

"Absolutely no eating it," said Tomi, licking his fingers.

The three of them climbed in, fastened their liquorice seat belts and counted together:

"Three! Two! One!"

And then… blastoff!

The candy rocket rose through clouds of candyfloss, pink, yellow and pale blue. Tiny coloured sparks flew past the window, as if someone had shaken a tub of sprinkles.

Everything smelled of vanilla.

"I'm just going to taste a little bit of window," said Tomi. "To see if it works."

"Tomi!" said Noa and Sami together.

Up, up high, where the clouds came to an end, they met someone.

It was a tiny star, sitting all alone on the edge of a cloud. She was hardly shining at all. She was pale, like a candle going out.

"What's the matter?" Noa asked her.

"I'm hungry," said the star, in a very small voice. "Stars eat sugar dust, the kind that falls from the sweet clouds. But this year, none fell. And without sugar I can't shine. And if I can't shine, I can't find my place in the sky."

The three friends looked at each other.

Then they looked at their spaceship.

Their spaceship, made entirely of sweets.

"Rule number one…" Noa began.

"No eating the spaceship," said Sami. "But it doesn't say anything about giving it away."

Sami gave the star the biscuit door. The star took a bite: crunch!

Noa gave her a lollipop button. And Tomi, after thinking about it for a moment, gave her the gummy bears from the window. All except one.

"This one's the captain," he explained.

The star ate the lot. And she began to shine. A little at first. Then more. And in the end so much, so very much, that she lit up the whole sky, and let out a laugh of pure happiness.

The trouble was, now the rocket had a hole where the door used to be, and another where the buttons had been. And it began to wobble.

"Hold on tight!" said the star.

She threw them a beam of light, like a golden rope, and lowered them gently down through the clouds, until they were back in the garden. Just in time for dinner.

That night, the three friends looked up at the sky from the window.

There was a new star, brighter than all the others. And she gave them a wink.

"Goodnight, little star," they whispered.

"I've got something to confess," said Tomi, nearly asleep. "I ate the captain."
